value: For malaria, a climatological ENSO value outperformed the observed ONI on average, though not clearly (−0.010 nats per unit-year; 95% CI −0.020 to +0.001). Relative to the model without ENSO terms, the model with them scored −0.017 nats per unit-year with the observed ONI and −0.007 with a climatological value. Season-level gains with the observed ONI vary widely (SD 0.052 over 20 seasons); the two largest in absolute value, 2016 (−0.150) and 2020 (+0.099), account for most of that spread (61% of the squared deviations from the mean) rather than the mean, which is −0.016 without them.

value: For recorded heat deaths, a climatological ENSO value outperformed the observed ONI on average, though not clearly (−0.002 nats per unit-year; 95% CI −0.015 to +0.011). The gain of the model with ENSO terms over the model without them (+0.042 nats per unit-year with the observed ONI, +0.044 with a climatological value) is therefore not clearly attributable to the ENSO value (the 95% CI of the observed ONI's advantage over a climatological value reaches +0.011 nats per unit-year); it is consistent with the non-ENSO Indian Ocean Dipole term (September–November Dipole index) that the model also adds, although no model with the Dipole term and without the ENSO terms was fitted. Season-level gains with the observed ONI vary widely (SD 0.134 over 20 seasons); the two largest in absolute value, 2024 (+0.457) and 2020 (−0.311), account for most of that spread (87% of the squared deviations from the mean) rather than the mean, which is +0.038 without them. The June and September issues hold the September–November Dipole index and the lagged heat deaths at their observed values, which are not known at those issue times (the Dipole season is also incomplete at the November issue), so the forecast gains at those leads are not lead-time skill.
